sections.heading: 3.3.1. Frozen-Head Decoding Constraint.
sections.text: To keep <pause> representations interpretable, SPOT employs a frozen-head projection that maps <pause> states into a fixed vocabulary-induced space used for alignment. Given a hidden state h ∈ ℝ d h\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , we obtain a token distribution via the frozen LM head ( W , b ) (W,b) : (6) p ( ⋅ ∣ h ) = Softmax ( W h + b ) . p(\cdot\mid h)=\mathrm{Softmax}(Wh+b). Subsequently, h h is mapped to a soft embedding within the token embedding space by computing the expectation over this distribution: (7) ϕ ( h ) = p ( ⋅ ∣ h ) ⊤ E ∈ ℝ d . \phi(h)=p(\cdot\mid h)^{\top}E\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. During Stage I, the LM head ( W , b ) (W,b) and the embedding matrix E E remain frozen; consequently, ϕ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \phi(\cdot) constitutes a fixed vocabulary-induced mapping utilized throughout the alignment training process. Furthermore, the frozen-head distribution p ( ⋅ ∣ h ) p(\cdot\mid h) enables the association of a hidden state with a concise set of high-probability vocabulary items. Let TopK ⁡ ( p , K ) \mathrm{TopK}(p,K) denote the set of indices corresponding to the K K most probable vocabulary items under distribution p p . For a given hidden state h h , we define (8) 𝒯 K ( h ) = TopK ( p ( ⋅ ∣ h ) , K ) , \mathcal{T}_{K}(h)\;=\;\mathrm{TopK}\!\bigl(p(\cdot\mid h),K\bigr), and utilize 𝒯 K ​ ( h ) \mathcal{T}_{K}(h) as a compact lexical summary of the semantic content encoded by h h (with K = 20 K{=}20 set as the default).

sections.heading: 3.3.2. Span-level Semantic Alignment.
sections.text: For each dropped span S i S_{i} ( i ∈ 𝒟 i\in\mathcal{D} ), the student model generates a single hidden state z i ∈ ℝ d z_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} at the corresponding <pause> position. In contrast, the teacher model yields a sequence of token-level hidden states corresponding to the same span, denoted by { h t tea } y t ∈ S i \{h^{\text{tea}}_{t}\}_{y_{t}\in S_{i}} . The objective is to align a single latent state with the semantics distributed across a variable-length span. This alignment is performed following the projection of both student and teacher states via the frozen-head mapping ϕ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \phi(\cdot) (Eq. ( 7 )), thereby embedding them into a shared semantic space. Specifically, the student state is mapped to (9) z ~ i = ϕ ⁡ ( z i ) ∈ ℝ d , \tilde{z}_{i}=\phi(z_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, while each teacher token state is transformed into h ~ t tea = ϕ ⁡ ( h t tea ) \tilde{h}^{\text{tea}}_{t}=\phi(h^{\text{tea}}_{t}) . Aggregating the projected teacher states yields the matrix: (10) H ~ tea ​ ( S i ) = [ h ~ t tea ] y t ∈ S i ∈ ℝ | S i | × d . \tilde{H}^{\text{tea}}(S_{i})=\big[\,\tilde{h}^{\text{tea}}_{t}\,\big]_{y_{t}\in S_{i}}\in\mathbb{R}^{|S_{i}|\times d}. To softly match a single <pause> state to a variable-length span, we use the Sinkhorn-regularized OT objective in Eq. ( 4 ) as a differentiable token-level set-matching loss between z ~ i \tilde{z}_{i} and { h ~ t tea } y t ∈ S i \{\tilde{h}^{\text{tea}}_{t}\}_{y_{t}\in S_{i}} . Given that the source distribution possesses a single support point, this one-to-span OT formulation simplifies to a weighted point-to-set distance —effectively distributing the unit mass from z ~ i \tilde{z}_{i} across the span tokens according to the target marginal—rather than a general many-to-many transport plan. Concretely, the ground cost between z ~ i \tilde{z}_{i} and each projected teacher token state is defined as follows: (11) C i ∈ ℝ + 1 × | S i | , ( C i ) 1 , t = ∥ z ~ i − h ~ t tea ∥ 2 2 , y t ∈ S i . C_{i}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{1\times|S_{i}|},\qquad(C_{i})_{1,t}=\bigl\lVert\tilde{z}_{i}-\tilde{h}^{\text{tea}}_{t}\bigr\rVert_{2}^{2},\quad y_{t}\in S_{i}. The source marginal concentrates all probability mass on the single <pause> state, whereas the target marginal assigns uniform mass across the tokens within the span: (12) a i = [ 1 ] ∈ Δ 1 , b i = 1 | S i | ​ 𝟏 ∈ Δ | S i | . a_{i}=[1]\in\Delta^{1},\qquad b_{i}=\frac{1}{|S_{i}|}\mathbf{1}\in\Delta^{|S_{i}|}. Finally, the span-level alignment loss is computed as the average of the Sinkhorn-regularized OT values over all dropped spans: (13) ℒ align = 1 | 𝒟 | ​ ∑ i ∈ 𝒟 OT ε ​ ( a i , b i , C i ) , \mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}\mathrm{OT}_{\varepsilon}\!\left(a_{i},\,b_{i};\,C_{i}\right), where OT ε ​ ( a , b , C ) \mathrm{OT}_{\varepsilon}(a,b;C) denotes the optimal value of Eq. ( 4 ). In this formulation, the alignment leverages all token states within the teacher span, thereby providing richer supervision compared to endpoint-only matching or simple pooling-based regression, while maintaining compatibility with variable span lengths.

sections.heading: 3.4.1. Stage I: OT alignment training.
sections.text: Given a SpanDrop sequence y ~ = ( y ~ 1 , … , y ~ T ~ ) \tilde{y}=(\tilde{y}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{y}_{\tilde{T}}) , we optimize the student model in Stage I using a composite objective comprising (i) an autoregressive next-token prediction loss on observed tokens and (ii) the span-level alignment loss defined in Eq. ( 13 ). In Stage I, we freeze the pretrained LM head ( W , b ) (W,b) and the token embedding matrix E E , and optimize the remaining student parameters θ \theta with the objective below. The next-token prediction loss is applied exclusively to non- <pause> tokens: (14) ℒ CE = − ∑ t = 1 T ~ 𝟏 [ y ~ t ≠ <pause> ] log p θ ( y ~ t ∣ x , y ~ < t ) . \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}=-\sum_{t=1}^{\tilde{T}}\mathbf{1}[\tilde{y}_{t}\neq\texttt{ }]\,\log p_{\theta}\!\left(\tilde{y}_{t}\mid x,\tilde{y}_{ The indicator function 𝟏 [ y ~ t ≠ <pause> ] \mathbf{1}[\tilde{y}_{t}\neq\texttt{ }] masks the <pause> positions, thereby preventing the cross-entropy term from imposing token-level supervision on the <pause> token itself. We combine ℒ CE \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}} with the alignment loss ℒ align \mathcal{L}_{\text{align}} (Eq. ( 13 )) as follows: (15) ℒ stage1 = ℒ CE + λ ​ ℒ align , \mathcal{L}_{\text{stage1}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}+\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}, where λ \lambda controls the relative strength of span-level alignment. Crucially, Stage I imposes no cross-entropy supervision at <pause> positions; rather, the <pause> token is introduced via the SpanDrop construction and serves as part of the conditioning context. Its hidden state is shaped solely through the span-level alignment objective. Consequently, the model is not trained to emit <pause> according to a fixed template. Instead, it learns to utilize <pause> as a carrier of internal computation, allowing inference-time insertion patterns to be specified externally to adjust the degree of implicit reasoning.

sections.heading: 3.4.2. Stage II: RFT stabilization.
sections.text: Although Stage I induces span-aligned <pause> representations, the trained model may remain sensitive to the specific placement and density of <pause> tokens inserted externally during inference. Stage II implements Rejection-Sampled Fine-Tuning (RFT) to improve robustness against such variations. For each input query x x , we first generate an uncompressed reference completion y ( 0 ) y^{(0)} that contains no <pause> tokens. Subsequently, we sample a set of candidate completions { y ( k ) } k = 1 K cand \{y^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K_{\text{cand}}} by inserting <pause> tokens according to various predefined patterns. A rejection step filters out candidates that yield incorrect final answers. Among the remaining correct candidates, we prioritize shorter outputs based on the scoring function: (16) s ⁡ ( y ( k ) , x ) = 1 − | y ( k ) | | y ( 0 ) | , s\!\left(y^{(k)};x\right)=1-\frac{|y^{(k)}|}{|y^{(0)}|}, where | ⋅ | |\cdot| denotes the output length. The candidate with the highest score is selected as the RFT target y ^ \hat{y} . The model is then fine-tuned on y ^ \hat{y} using the same next-token prediction loss: (17) ℒ RFT = − ∑ t = 1 | y ^ | 𝟏 [ y ^ t ≠ <pause> ] log p θ ( y ^ t ∣ x , y ^ < t ) . \mathcal{L}_{\text{RFT}}=-\sum_{t=1}^{|\hat{y}|}\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{t}\neq\texttt{ }]\,\log p_{\theta}\!\left(\hat{y}_{t}\mid x,\hat{y}_{ Consistent with Stage I, the indicator 𝟏 [ y ^ t ≠ <pause> ] \mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{t}\neq\texttt{ }] ensures that the cross-entropy loss does not treat <pause> as a prediction target. However, Stage II explicitly allows the optimization of the embedding vector for <pause> , which empirically improves the stability of generations conditioned on externally inserted <pause> tokens. During RFT, we keep ( W , b ) (W,b) frozen and freeze E E except for the <pause> embedding. All remaining trainable parameters are the same θ \theta optimized in Stage I.

sections.heading: 3.5. Inference-time insertion.
sections.text: During inference, we externally inject <pause> tokens into the reasoning segment (for DeepSeek-style outputs, the <think> … </think> region) at intervals of N N spans (defined in Section 2 ), and never insert <pause> outside this segment. This mechanism affords explicit control over the extent to which intermediate computation is performed implicitly, while preserving the native response format of the model. SPOT also supports more flexible insertion rules; see Appendix A.1 for further discussion.

sections.heading: 4.1.3. Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: Prompt templates and task-specific answer format constraints are provided in Appendix A.3 . Decoding uses temperature 0.6 0.6 , top- p p 0.95 0.95 , and a maximum generation length of 16,384 tokens. All reported results are averaged over ten decoding runs with different random seeds. In the main results, we use N = 3 N{=}3 on all math benchmarks and N = 1 N{=}1 on GPQA-Diamond, where N N is the number of explicit spans between two consecutive inference-time <pause> insertions (Section 3.5 ).

sections.heading: 4.1.5. Baselines
sections.text: We compare SPOT with representative baselines under the same DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B backbone. Vanilla denotes the original model without intervention. We include explicit trace-control baselines (CCoT ( Renze and Guven, 2024 ) , ConciseHint ( Tang et al., 2025 ) , Step Entropy ( Li et al., 2025b ) , L1-Max ( Aggarwal and Welleck, 2025 ) , DEER ( Yang et al., 2025 ) ) and implicit/latent baselines (COCONUT ( Hao et al., 2025b ) , CODI ( Shen et al., 2025 ) , LightThinker ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , Latent-SFT ( Deng et al., 2025 ) ). Detailed descriptions are in Appendix A.4 .

sections.heading: 4.2. Implementation Details
sections.text: Experiments are run on a single machine with 2 × 2\times NVIDIA RTX 5880 Ada GPUs (48 GB each) and dual-socket Intel Xeon Gold 6454S CPUs. Training uses PyTorch with the HuggingFace Transformers framework and Distributed Data Parallel (DDP) across two GPUs. We train the model with bfloat16 precision. Training configuration. Stage I uses a maximum sequence length of 4096, per-device batch size 1, and gradient accumulation of 8. Optimization uses AdamW for 5 epochs with learning rate 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} , warmup ratio 0.05, and max gradient norm 1.0. For Sinkhorn OT, we set blur =0.05 and scaling =0.9. Unless stated otherwise, we set λ = 1.0 \lambda=1.0 (Eq. 15 ), and each teacher span is capped at 256 token states with uniform subsampling when exceeded. Stage II (RFT) follows the same optimizer settings. Parameter-efficient adaptation. In both stages, we fine-tune the student model using LoRA while keeping the teacher model frozen. We use LoRA rank r = 64 r{=}64 , scaling α = 128 \alpha{=}128 , and dropout 0.1, applied to the linear projections in the attention blocks ( q , k , v , o q,k,v,o ) and the MLP layers (gate/up/down). The LM head is kept frozen throughout; in Stage II, we additionally unfreeze the embedding vector of <pause> while keeping all other token embeddings frozen. sections.heading: 4.3. Main Results
sections.text: As shown in Table 1 , SPOT substantially shortens generation while matching or exceeding the accuracy of the Vanilla backbone. By contrast, existing efficiency baselines often yield only modest length reductions, and their accuracy degradation becomes more apparent on harder benchmarks. Specifically, SPOT reduces output length by 52.1% on GSM8K and 43.0% on MATH500 while improving accuracy by +3.1 and +1.4 points, respectively. The improvements persist on more challenging and out-of-domain settings: On the harder AIME2025 benchmark, SPOT-stage2 achieves 39.33% accuracy (+3.3 points) while generating 15.8% fewer tokens, and it generalizes to out-of-domain GPQA-Diamond with 54.55% accuracy (+4.5 points) alongside a 49.3% reduction in output length. Overall, SPOT achieves strong compression without the pronounced accuracy drop often observed in aggressive explicit shortening or fully latent compression baselines, and Stage II further stabilizes this behavior, yielding the best results among SPOT variants.

Ablation on the alignment objective. Each #L cell reports the absolute length with a subscript showing relative change vs. Vanilla. Table 2 shows that the alignment objective is critical. We compare Sinkhorn OT with two heuristic alternatives that use the same frozen-head projection space. End_KL provides endpoint-only supervision by forcing the <pause> state to match the frozen-head decoding distribution of the last teacher token in the span. MSE uses a pooled target by averaging the teacher span into a single representation and regressing the <pause> state to this average, which ignores token-level structure within the span. Replacing Sinkhorn OT with End_KL or MSE leads to clear accuracy drops, with the largest degradation on the hardest math benchmark (AIME2025). These alternatives can also weaken length control on difficult settings, yielding longer generations (e.g., MSE on AIME2025 and GPQA-Diamond). In contrast, Sinkhorn OT achieves the most favorable accuracy–length profile across the three benchmarks, supporting its role as a robust many-to-one alignment between a single <pause> state and a variable-length teacher span.

sections.heading: 4.5.2. LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation of Compressed Reasoning
sections.text: To further test whether externally inserted <pause> tokens act as a latent carrier for non-trivial compression, we adopt an LLM-as-a-Judge protocol that scores text locally around each <pause> boundary. Under the same inference-time insertion schedule (Section 3.5 ), we extract boundary pairs ( PREVIOUS_SPAN , NEXT_SPAN ) (\texttt{PREVIOUS\_SPAN},\texttt{NEXT\_SPAN}) , where spans are paragraphs in <think> (split by \n\n ). The judge assigns two 1–5 scores. pause_utilization measures whether NEXT_SPAN relies on an intermediate conclusion not stated in PREVIOUS_SPAN , i.e., evidence of a meaningful jump across the <pause> token. local_continuity measures whether NEXT_SPAN remains consistent with PREVIOUS_SPAN (allowing a minimal bridge), penalizing contradictions or broken variable tracking. We report mean scores and Joint@4 , the fraction of boundaries where both scores are ≥ 4 \geq 4 (Appendix A.7 ). As shown in Table 5 , SPOT improves pause_utilization over the vanilla backbone while maintaining high local_continuity , resulting in a much higher Joint@4 . This indicates that <pause> more often coincides with meaningful compression gaps under SPOT, without disrupting local coherence.
